title: WIFE OR CONCUBINE? Why Some Biblical Women Are Described Differently in Different Passages
paragraphs:
WIFE OR CONCUBINE? Why Some Biblical Women Are Described Differently in Different Passages
One woman can be called a “wife” in one passage and a “concubine” in another—and that does not mean the Bible contradicted itself. What if the apparent discrepancy is actually revealing something painful about the ancient world, something important about how Scripture tells the truth, and something breathtaking about the kind of people Jesus came to redeem?
You are reading your Bible when suddenly something feels wrong.
You stop.
You go back.
You read the verse again.
Wait...
Wasn’t she his wife?
Why does another passage call her his concubine?
And if you have ever noticed this, you are not asking a foolish question.
You are noticing something real.
Genesis 25:1 introduces Keturah using language commonly translated:
“Abraham took another wife, and her name was Keturah.”
The Hebrew noun behind “wife” is:
אִשָּׁה — ’iššâ
It can mean “woman” or “wife,” depending on context.
But then you reach 1 Chronicles 1:32, and suddenly Keturah is described differently:
“The sons of Keturah, Abraham’s concubine...”
Now the Hebrew word is:
פִּילֶגֶשׁ — pîlegeš
“Concubine.”
Same Keturah.
Same Abraham.
Different description.
Contradiction?
No.
And understanding why opens a window into something much larger than vocabulary.
It opens a window into the difference between what Scripture records and what Scripture approves, between relationship and social status, between God’s design and humanity’s distortion of it.
And ultimately...
between scandal and grace.
Because the Bible does something religious propaganda usually refuses to do.
It tells the truth about its own people.
It does not airbrush Abraham.
It does not sanitize Jacob.
It does not hide David’s household.
It does not turn dysfunctional families into stained-glass saints.
Scripture can tell you that Abraham believed God—and then show you Abraham making disastrous choices.
It can call David a man after God’s heart and still devote entire chapters to the devastation caused by David’s sin.
It can preserve the names of women whom the ancient world might have preferred to leave unnamed.
That honesty matters.
And it begins all the way back at creation.
Before kings accumulated wives...
before servants were given to husbands...
before royal harems...
before concubines...
before inheritance disputes...
before human beings complicated marriage with power, politics, lust, fear, infertility, status, and survival...
there was Eden.
Genesis 2:24 gives the foundational picture:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
One man.
His wife.
One-flesh covenant union.
Jesus Himself reaches back to this creation account when questioned about marriage. He does not point His hearers toward David’s household or Solomon’s harem as the ideal.
He points backward.
To the beginning.
“Have you not read...?”
Then Christ cites Genesis and declares:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
That distinction is essential when reading the Old Testament.
The presence of something in Scripture is not automatically the endorsement of that thing by Scripture.
The Bible records murder.
It does not endorse murder.
The Bible records adultery.
It does not endorse adultery.
The Bible records deception, slavery, warfare, idolatry, polygamy, exploitation, betrayal, drunkenness, revenge, sexual violence, and grotesque abuses of power.
Its willingness to describe humanity truthfully should never be mistaken for divine approval of everything humanity does.
That brings us back to the mysterious word:
פִּילֶגֶשׁ — pîlegeš
Usually rendered “concubine.”
Its ultimate etymology is uncertain, so we should resist impressive-sounding theories that claim more certainty than the evidence permits.

But its biblical usage is clear enough to show that a pîlegeš occupied a recognized relationship with a man while generally possessing a different or secondary status from what English readers normally imagine when they hear “wife.”
That distinction explains something easily lost in translation.
“Concubine” did not necessarily mean what a modern reader might mean by “mistress.”
These women were not automatically secret adulterous partners hidden outside a household.
They could belong to an established household relationship, yet occupy a subordinate social position.
That is precisely why the Bible can sometimes use language that sounds confusing to modern ears.
A woman might be described according to her relationship in one context and according to her rank or status in another.
Keturah demonstrates this vividly.
Genesis calls her Abraham’s ’iššâ.
Chronicles calls her his pîlegeš.
Genesis 25:6 also speaks of Abraham’s “concubines” when explaining how Abraham distributed gifts while reserving the primary inheritance for Isaac.
The point is not that words suddenly ceased to mean anything.
The point is that ancient household categories do not fit perfectly into our modern English boxes.
And Keturah is not the only woman whose description demands careful reading.
Consider Hagar.
She enters Abraham’s story as Sarah’s Egyptian servant.
Genesis 16 identifies her with the Hebrew:
שִׁפְחָה — šip̄ḥâ
A female servant or maidservant.
Sarah, unable to conceive, gives Hagar to Abraham.
Genesis 16:3 then uses striking language: Sarah gives Hagar to Abram “as a wife.”
Again we encounter:
אִשָּׁה — ’iššâ
But Hagar does not thereby become socially identical to Sarah.
That becomes painfully obvious almost immediately.
Pregnancy changes the household.
Jealousy erupts.
Power is abused.
Hagar suffers.
She runs.
And then comes one of Scripture’s most beautiful reversals.
The woman who had become socially useful to Abraham’s household...
the woman caught in somebody else’s desperate attempt to manufacture God’s promise...
the woman mistreated badly enough to flee into the wilderness...
is found by God.
Not because the human arrangement was ideal.
Not because everything Abraham and Sarah had done was justified.
But because God sees people whom powerful people reduce to roles.
Hagar gives the LORD a name associated with the God who sees her.
Think about that.
People saw a servant.
People saw fertility.
People saw a solution.
People saw a problem.
God saw Hagar.
Maybe that is where this ancient question suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because perhaps you know what it feels like to be known mainly by your usefulness.
Employee.
Mother.
Father.
Provider.
Divorcee.
Widow.
Failure.
Addict.
Problem child.
Single mother.
Former inmate.
The difficult one.
The disappointing one.
The person everyone calls when they need something but somehow forget when you are bleeding.
Human beings are very good at reducing people to categories.
God keeps calling people by name.
Then there are Bilhah and Zilpah.
Their stories emerge from Jacob’s fractured household.
Rachel and Leah become trapped in a devastating competition for children and affection. Their female servants become part of that rivalry, bearing children to Jacob.
The result is not a glowing advertisement for polygamous domestic bliss.
Read the story slowly.
There is jealousy.
Competition.
Favoritism.
Bargaining.
Heartache.
Children born into rivalry.
A husband pulled through a household filled with emotional fractures.
And eventually those fractures spill into the next generation.
Joseph is favored.
His brothers resent him.
A coat becomes a symbol.
A pit appears.
A brother is sold.
A father grieves.
A family nearly destroys itself.
The Bible does not need to insert a footnote saying, “This household arrangement has consequences.”
The narrative shows you the consequences.
Then Scripture takes us somewhere even darker.
Judges 19.
A Levite has a pîlegeš.
A concubine.

But within the same narrative, familial terminology associated with marriage appears around their relationship: the woman’s father functions as the man’s father-in-law, and the text presents a recognized household bond.
Then everything collapses into horror.
The woman is subjected to brutal sexual violence.
She dies.
Her body is desecrated.
Israel descends toward civil war.
Judges 19 is not a chapter designed to make you comfortable.
It is supposed to make you recoil.
And its placement within Judges matters.
The book repeatedly drives toward the terrifying diagnosis:
“In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”
Judges is showing what human beings become when covenant faithfulness collapses.
So when we encounter the concubine in Judges 19, the question cannot merely be:
“What was her technical marital classification?”
There is a more haunting question.
What happens when human beings stop seeing another person as someone bearing the image of God?
She becomes negotiable.
Disposable.
A means of self-preservation.
A body rather than a person.
And suddenly an ancient story feels frighteningly contemporary.
Because our civilization may use different vocabulary, but human beings still objectify.
Still exploit.
Still consume.
Still discard.
Still hide abuse behind respectability.
Still know how to appear religious while somebody inside the house is being destroyed.
You can know Bible verses and still fail to love your wife.
You can post Christian content and still humiliate your husband.
You can raise your hands in worship and treat someone made in God’s image as disposable.
You can defend biblical marriage publicly while destroying your own marriage privately through pornography, cruelty, adultery, manipulation, neglect, pride, or unforgiveness.
That is where this stops being an ancient Hebrew word study.
Because Scripture was never given merely so we could win arguments about people who died three thousand years ago.
The Word eventually turns the light toward us.
Maybe your scandal does not involve concubines.
Maybe yours lives in browser history.
Maybe it lives inside deleted messages.
Maybe it has another person’s name attached to it.
Maybe nobody knows about the emotional affair.
Maybe everybody thinks your marriage is beautiful because they only see the photographs.
Maybe you have learned Christian vocabulary well enough to conceal a heart that has wandered miles from Christ.
Maybe you have never physically committed adultery, but Jesus’ words about lust leave you nowhere comfortable to hide.
Maybe you are not the person who caused the wound.
Maybe you are Hagar in the wilderness.
Used.
Rejected.
Confused.
Wondering whether God saw what happened.
Maybe you are carrying wounds from a relationship where somebody invoked God while treating you in a way that did not resemble Him.
Hear this carefully:
The sins of biblical characters are not permission slips for ours.
“Abraham did it” is not a theology of marriage.
“David had multiple wives” is not Christ’s command.
“Solomon had concubines” does not make Solomon’s household God’s blueprint.
In fact, Solomon becomes one of Scripture’s clearest warnings.
First Kings tells us that his wives turned his heart toward other gods.
The king famous for wisdom became living proof that possessing biblical knowledge does not guarantee an undivided heart.
That should frighten every religious person just enough to become humble.
You can know truth and still wander.
You can teach truth and still wander.
You can build something impressive and still wander.
You can look spiritually successful while your heart quietly develops another altar.
And that is why Christianity is not ultimately the announcement that morally impressive people should try harder.
It is the announcement that sinners need a Savior.

The Bible's tangled marriages, broken households, abused women, compromised patriarchs, fallen kings, jealous siblings, desperate mothers, lustful men, wounded families, and catastrophic decisions all testify to one enormous truth:
Humanity cannot save itself.
We need Someone better than Abraham.
Someone purer than David.
Someone wiser than Solomon.
Someone who will not exploit the vulnerable.
Someone who will not abandon the wounded.
Someone whose covenant faithfulness will not collapse when ours does.
And then Jesus walks onto the pages of history.
Look at the women surrounding His story.
Women society whispered about.
Women carrying complicated histories.
Women considered ceremonially unclean.
Women whose reputations entered rooms before they did.
A Samaritan woman with a shattered relational history meets Him beside a well.
Jesus knows.
Everything.
And yet He speaks to her.
Not with sentimental approval of sin.
Not with contempt.
With truth.
With exposure.
With an invitation to living water.
That is Jesus.
He does not call darkness light.
He turns on the light so people can finally walk out of darkness.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace cost blood.
At the cross, Jesus Christ bears judgment for sinners.
The innocent One stands where the guilty should stand.
The faithful Bridegroom gives Himself for His people.
Paul later reaches for the language of marriage when describing Christ and the church:
“Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
There is the Husband humanity could never manufacture.
Faithful.
Sacrificial.
Holy.
Truthful.
Merciful.
He does not exploit His Bride.
He dies for her.
And this is why biblical marriage finally makes sense only when Christ stands at the center.
Marriage was never ultimately about male domination.
Never about collecting women.
Never about social prestige.
Never about using another human being to satisfy appetite.
Christian marriage points beyond itself toward covenant faithfulness—the mystery Paul connects to Christ and His church.
That does not erase the difficult Old Testament texts.
It helps us locate them within the whole biblical story.
Creation gives us the design.
Human sin fractures it.
Israel's history shows how deep the fracture goes.
The prophets expose unfaithfulness.
Jesus restores our eyes to God's intention.
The cross reveals covenant love at unimaginable cost.
And redemption moves toward the marriage supper of the Lamb.
From Genesis to Revelation, marriage imagery ultimately reaches beyond Abraham, Sarah, Hagar, Keturah, Jacob, Rachel, Leah, Bilhah, Zilpah, David, Solomon, or any other flawed human household.
It reaches Christ.
Which means perhaps the most important question after studying “wife or concubine?” is not merely:
“What category did this particular ancient woman occupy?”
The question eventually becomes:
Where do I stand before the Bridegroom?
Because you can solve every Hebrew vocabulary question in this article and remain spiritually dead.
You can understand אִשָּׁה and פִּילֶגֶשׁ perfectly and still refuse Jesus.
You can defend marriage and never surrender your lust.
You can condemn somebody else's scandal while protecting your own.
The Gospel does not invite us merely to analyze broken people.
It calls broken people to repentance.
Including me.
Including you.
Jesus did not come because respectable people needed religious accessories.
He came because sinners needed resurrection.
So bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the marriage barely breathing behind closed doors.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the adultery.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the memories you cannot erase.
Bring Him the wounds somebody else caused.
Bring Him the religious hypocrisy.
Bring Him the part of your story you desperately hope nobody ever reads aloud.
Repent where you have sinned.
Seek forgiveness.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Get help where the damage is deeper than you can repair alone.
And when you are the wounded rather than the offender, understand that forgiveness does not require pretending evil was acceptable or remaining in danger.
Bring the truth into the light.
Because Jesus Christ specializes in meeting people where scandal said their story should end.
Peter denied Him.
Christ restored him.
Paul persecuted His church.
Christ transformed him.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated past.
Christ offered living water.
The thief beside Jesus was running out of minutes.
Christ gave him paradise.
This is Christianity.
Not good people congratulating themselves.
Dead people being made alive by Jesus Christ.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And maybe while reading this, something got uncomfortably close.
If you need repentance, repent.
If you need prayer, ask.
If you have been hiding, come into the light.

And if Christ has already taken a chapter of your life that looked ruined and begun turning it into a testimony, tell somebody below what He did. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer desperately needed tonight.
Not because every paragraph was comfortable.
Because some truths need to be reread when temptation, confusion, shame, or spiritual forgetfulness returns.
Not as religious decoration.
Let them discover what the Bible actually contains:
Broken human beings.
A holy God.
Real judgment.
Costly mercy.
And a Savior powerful enough to redeem what sin has devastated.
Grace cannot be bought.
But ministry can be supported.
If these messages keep meeting you in places nobody else sees, stay close.
But before you leave, remember the woman whose title changed depending on the passage.
“Wife.”
“Concubine.”
“Servant.”
Human history has always been full of labels.
Maybe yours is too.
Divorced.
Rejected.
Unwanted.
Unfaithful.
Abused.
Addicted.
Ashamed.
Failure.
Too far gone.
But none of those words has the authority to write the final sentence of a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
The cross gets the final word.
Grace gets the final word.
Christ gets the final word.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your story—but when Jesus takes the pen, your scandal does not get to write the ending.
